THE CURATOR’S NOTE↓
[ MANIFESTO ]

A different way
to imagine.

Some games ask you to win.
Others change the way you see.

There has never been just one French style. There is, however, a restless impulse: to borrow from cinema, illustration, architecture, and music—and make something that could only exist through play.

This is a journey through that impulse. From 8-bit experiments to painted worlds, meet the people who made the screen a canvas.

UNE HISTOIRE
À JOUER ↗
PROLOGUE / BEFORE THE FIRST STUDIOS1970s—1985

Before a signature,
a screen.

The story begins with access. To a machine. To a language. To the possibility of making something yourself.

INSERT A COIN.
LOAD A CASSETTE.
WRITE A FIRST LINE.
1970s
THE SCREEN ENTERS EVERYDAY LIFE

A new kind
of public space.

Arcade machines and early home consoles introduce a new relationship with the moving image: the spectator can act. In France, as elsewhere, a culture of playing takes shape before a recognisable local production industry.

1980s
FROM CONSUMER TO CREATOR

The keyboard
changes the equation.

A home computer can run a game and make one. Shops, importers, specialist magazines, and hobbyists connect the two activities. The cassette travels through a social network long before the web: discovery, advice, distribution, and the first independent publishers.

Historical lens / Colin Sidre’s research places these often overlooked intermediaries at the centre of the early French scene.

1985
INFORMATIQUE POUR TOUS

A computer becomes
a public question.

Presented on 25 January 1985, the national plan brings equipment, teacher training, and public access into the same conversation. It is part of the context in which the Thomson generation encounters computing—alongside the home, the shop, and the games magazine.

01 / THE FIRST PIXELS1980—1989

Small rooms.
Infinite worlds.

Before the industry, there was curiosity.
And a computer on the kitchen table.

1983
CHAPTER I // THE BEDROOM PIONEERS

Oric-1. Thomson MO5. Amstrad CPC.
Limited memory. Unlimited possibility.

ILLUSTRATION / A HOME-COMPUTING MEMORY
1983 // A SCENE IS BORN

The first
independents.

Loriciels and Infogrames are founded in 1983. Around the Oric and other home micros, hobbyists become authors, and authors become publishers. Infogrames’ armadillo will become one of the era’s most recognisable signatures.

1984 // THE HOME BECOMES A STUDIO

A keyboard.
A blank canvas.

The Thomson MO5 arrives in 1984. Alongside the Amstrad CPC and the Oric, it opens a space for local software, strange adventures, and inventive visual languages. Games circulate on cassettes; their creators learn by making.

THOMSON MO548 KB RAM / 1984
1985—1989 // FROM IMPULSE TO INDUSTRY

The map
gets bigger.

Titus is founded in 1985. In Brittany, the Guillemot brothers establish Ubisoft in 1986. The creative scene grows beyond individual bedrooms into a network of studios, publishers, and new possibilities.

COUNTERPOINT / 1987—1988

Other worlds.
Other points of view.

The early adventure game is already more than a technical experiment. It can carry a particular history—or make understanding another being the adventure itself.

01 / MARTINIQUE1987

Méwilo.

Muriel Tramis / Coktel Vision

With Patrick Chamoiseau and Philippe Truca, Tramis creates an investigation rooted in Saint-Pierre in 1902. Caribbean culture and historical memory enter the game’s imaginative world. The geography of French production is wider than metropolitan France.

02 / AN ALIEN LANGUAGE1988

Captain Blood.

ERE Informatique / Exxos

An exploration game asks the player to communicate with alien inhabitants. The encounter is strange, and understanding is part of the task. A different ambition emerges: make the unfamiliar a language to learn.

ARCHIVAL DATA / 001

A creative critical mass.

Eight years. Seven foundations.
A scene finding its own voice.

1982BEFORE THE FIRST FOUNDATIONS

Before the big bang.

Before the names on this graph, there is a culture of experimentation. Home computers offer a personal space to learn, draw, and make games. This year is our starting point, not the beginning of French gaming.

When pixels
became poetry.

Five works. Five ways of seeing.
A generation that rewrote the rules.

INTERLUDE / THE MULTIMEDIA YEARS1994—1997

The CD-ROM opens
another room.

Illustration, voices, music, and reconstructed places become material for an adventure. The decade’s history unfolds beyond a single genre.

L’ART DU JEU
INTERACTIVE ARCHIVE
VOL. 02 / 1990s

A change in medium, many possible directions. The cultural adventure, the imagined civilisation, and the small hero in a large world.

AN ORIGINAL EDITORIAL STUDY / NOT A GAME DISC
1994

Little Big Adventure.

Adeline Software

Twinsen’s journey brings together a distinctive viewpoint, a whimsical world, and the menace of Dr FunFrock. The team behind Little Big Adventure shows that the move into three dimensions can serve an individual visual imagination.

1996

Versailles 1685.

Cryo / Canal+ Multimedia / RMN

A collaboration between game creators and cultural institutions turns the palace into an interactive investigation. Historical knowledge and a mystery share the same space; the heritage site becomes somewhere to explore.

1997

Atlantis.

Cryo Interactive

A first-person adventure builds a lost civilisation through environments, voices, puzzles, and music. Following Dune, Cryo continues to test how an imagined world can be both an audiovisual work and a place to inhabit.

03 / WORLDS WITHOUT LIMITS2000—2015
FROM AUTHORSHIP TO ARCHITECTURE

The world
is the work.

The canvas expands. So does the ambition.

Ubisoft turns open worlds into a global language. Arkane builds places that answer back. Quantic Dream explores interactive cinema; DON’T NOD makes memory, adolescence, and consequence playable.

FOUR APPROACHES
2002—2012 / A WIDER FIELD

Many ways
to build a world.

The adventure continues. Racing becomes a construction kit. An online universe grows beyond its launch. Strategy makes the rules themselves a form of world-building.

2002
MICROIDS / BENOÎT SOKAL

Syberia.

Kate Walker’s journey carries the adventure tradition into a new decade. Sokal’s composed environments, mechanical imagination, and attention to atmosphere sustain a different tempo from the expanding action world.

THE AUTHORED
JOURNEY
2003
UBISOFT MONTPELLIER

Beyond Good & Evil.

Jade’s investigation combines action with a journalist’s search for evidence. The game complicates the divide between a major publisher and a distinctive creative voice: a studio inside a global organisation can propose its own way of seeing.

THE WORLD
AS EVIDENCE
2003
NADEO

Trackmania.

The player does more than drive. Building and sharing tracks extends authorship into the community. A racing game becomes a renewable collection of routes, records, and experiments made by the people who play it.

THE PLAYER
AS DESIGNER
2004
ANKAMA / ROUBAIX

DOFUS.

The World of Twelve becomes a place to return to together. Ankama’s online role-playing game connects with a broader universe of comics and animation, while its continuing community makes the launch date a beginning rather than an ending.

THE SHARED
UNIVERSE
2012
AMPLITUDE STUDIOS

Endless Space.

Turn-based 4X strategy expresses a galaxy through systems and choices. Exploration and the development of a civilisation offer another scale of imagination—one in which the world is also the relationship between its rules.

THE SYSTEM
AS WORLD
CURATORIAL STUDY / 002

A signature in motion.

Four resonances. One restless imagination.
A living study of La French Touch.

01 / VISUAL CULTURE

Beyond the
drawn panel.

Bande dessinée offers a way to think in striking compositions, expressive silhouettes, and worlds suggested beyond the frame. Another World and Rayman take radically different routes through that visual imagination.

THE RESONANCE

Composition becomes a language. A silhouette can tell a story before a word is spoken.

Independent minds.

THREE MORE VOICES / 2016—2023

Independence
has many accents.

A concentrated duel. A body learning through repetition. A language slowly understood. Smaller productions can make a single idea feel like an entire world.

01
2016THE GAME BAKERS

Furi.

Sword fighting and twin-stick shooting become a sequence of exacting encounters. Takashi Okazaki’s character designs and an electronic soundtrack turn concentration, rhythm, and resolve into a vivid collaborative work.

02
2022SLOCLAP / PARIS

Sifu.

A Paris studio builds an action game around martial-arts combat and practice. Its international references make an essential point: a history of where games are made is also a history of influences crossing borders.

03
2023RUNDISC / TOULOUSE

Chants of Sennaar.

In a Babel-inspired tower, deciphering languages is the route forward. Observation and interpretation bring divided groups into focus. Understanding another person becomes the adventure’s central action.

The technology changes.
The need to create remains.

L’ART DU JEU / A CURATORIAL REFLECTION
CONTEXT / THE PEOPLE BEHIND THE SCREENPRESERVE · TEACH · SUPPORT

A culture needs
a memory.

Games do not survive through nostalgia alone. They need archives, skills passed between generations, and the conditions in which new work can be made.

Authorship is collective. Programmers, artists, writers, designers, composers, testers, publishers, and players all belong to this history. “La French Touch” is a lens through which to look, not a boundary around who can contribute.

1992 / 199301 / KEEP THE WORK

The game enters
the archive.

France extends legal deposit to electronic documents through the 1992 law and its 1993 implementing decree. The BnF’s game collections preserve software across changing physical formats, together with documentation that helps future researchers understand it. A cassette or cartridge becomes evidence of a culture, as well as a way to play.

BnF / games in the collections ↗
2001 / 200402 / PASS ON THE CRAFT

Making games
becomes a course.

The programme that leads to Cnam-Enjmin begins as a DESS in 2001 and becomes a master’s degree in 2004. Its history links the Cnam, the universities of Poitiers and La Rochelle, and Angoulême’s image culture. The bedroom narrative expands into another history: learning to create as a multidisciplinary team.

Cnam-Enjmin / the programme’s history ↗
200803 / MAKE ROOM FOR CREATION

Culture meets
production.

Established in 2008, the French video game tax credit places game creation within a framework of cultural and industrial support. It is one part of the context surrounding the works in these rooms. Their history is shaped by institutions and production conditions, as well as by artistic choices.

CNC / a historical account of the scheme ↗

THE CURATORIAL FILE
TRANSPARENCY / CONTEXT / CREDIT

Behind
the exhibition.

This independent exhibition is a selective cultural history, not a complete survey. “La French Touch” is used as a curatorial lens, not a claim that every French studio shares a single style.

About the studio chart

The chart counts only these selected foundations: Loriciels and Infogrames (1983), Coktel Vision (1984), Titus (1985), Ubisoft (1986), Lankhor (1987), and Delphine Software (1988). Its baseline is 1982. It does not measure active companies, market size, or the full French industry.

Image credits

Game imagery is used to identify and discuss the exhibited works. Rights remain with their owners. Another World and Flashback are shown using later commercial editions; Rayman is represented by the Rayman Forever collection. The dates in the exhibition refer to original releases.

    Sound & accessibility

    The optional ambient sound is an original, procedural synthesizer composition. It begins only when enabled. Reduced-motion preferences disable momentum, pinned sequences, image distortions, and cursor effects. All exhibits can be opened with a keyboard.
